children: Hugo Boss said its supervisory board chairman Stephan Sturm plans to step down after Frasers Group, the company's largest shareholder, reached near-majority ownership and said it would review whether to keep backing him.
The German premium-apparel company said Monday that Sturm's decision followed discussions against the backdrop of recent changes in the company's shareholder structure.

The move comes after U.K. retailer Frasers earlier this month said it was reviewing whether it would continue to support Sturm as chairman of Hugo Boss's supervisory board. Frasers also said that it aimed to achieve majority ownership in Hugo Boss, after a recent tender offer of 1.93 billion euros ($2.24 billion) for the shares it didn't already own left it with a 47.89% stake.

Frasers said Monday it discussed with Sturm an increase in its representation on the Hugo Boss supervisory board, and that both parties shared the view that it was an appropriate time to appoint a new chair.
"Following the recent changes in the company's shareholder structure, I believe that this is the right time for an orderly transition in the chairmanship," Sturm said.
Hugo Boss said its supervisory board would start immediately a process to name a new chair and Sturm's successor on the board.
Frasers said it would seek the appointment of Robert Palmer as a member of the supervisory board.

Sturm plans to continue as chair until a successor has been appointed but no later than Oct. 15, when he intends to step down from the supervisory board, the company said. He was elected to Hugo Boss's supervisory board in May last year and subsequently elected chair.
